Modelling growth data and other potentially negative response values

Source: vignettes/example7.Rmd
example7.Rmd

Summary

This vignette examines how different conventions for handling negative growth-rate measurements affect concentration-response modelling and the resulting toxicity estimates. Negative growth rates are common in algal toxicity tests and other ecological endpoints that measure change over time, yet many analytical workflows modify or remove these observations before model fitting.

Using simulated datasets where the true toxicity values are known, six commonly used approaches were compared: retaining measured values, censoring values below zero, deleting negative observations, replacing negatives with zero (“flooring”), and fitting Beta or Gamma response distributions that do not permit negative values. Performance was assessed for ErC10, ErC50 and NSEC estimates across a range of experimental designs and levels of measurement precision.

The results show that approaches which retain the measured information, either directly or through censoring, consistently recover the true toxicity values, maintain nominal interval coverage, and improve as experimental precision increases. Deleting negative observations performs less well but remains largely unbiased. In contrast, conventions that replace negative values or impose a non-negative response distribution introduce systematic bias that does not disappear with increasing precision. Flooring negative values produces increasingly over-conservative toxicity estimates, particularly for the NSEC, while Beta and Gamma models can introduce substantial bias despite successfully converging.

Application to four real algal growth datasets demonstrated that the choice of convention can materially affect reported toxicity values, although the magnitude of the effect depends on the prevalence of observations at or below zero growth. The simulation results indicate that the direction of the bias is predictable even when its magnitude is dataset specific.

Overall, the study supports analysing growth-rate data as measured whenever possible and using censoring when values below a detection or counting limit are unavailable. The results provide strong evidence against replacing negative values with zero or selecting bounded response distributions solely because negative responses are present. These practices distort the data-generating process and can produce toxicity estimates that become more confidently wrong as data quality improves.

1 Negative growth rates

Some ecotoxicological responses can legitimately take negative values. Specific growth rate is the most common example: as a rate of change, it is negative for a population that declines over the course of a test. Other examples include increments, differences between paired measurements, and any response expressed as a change from a baseline.

However, these negative values are typically removed before fitting, both in this package and in others. The reasons are long-standing, and none of them is specific to any one piece of software. A negative value cannot be expressed as a percentage of the control without the percentage exceeding 100, and several commonly used concentration-response equations cannot generate a negative mean at all. In addition, a negative growth rate looks anomalous on a plot, which may cause the reader to treat it as an error and not as a measurement.

The negative values are removed in one of several ways: by deleting the rows that hold them, by replacing them with zero before fitting, by declaring them censored at zero, or by fitting a response distribution that has no support below zero (e.g. a Beta or a Gamma). In a minority of cases the negative values are kept and the model is fitted to the data as recorded, which is the measured convention of Section 5.

Here we examine how each of these conventions affects the toxicity estimate that is subsequently reported. We first define the estimates and explain why their definition is important when the response can cross zero (Section 2), and then set out what replacing a negative value commits the analyst to, which is more than an edit to the data (Section 3). We also list the equations bayesnec fits under a Gaussian family, and the ECx that ecx() returns for them (Section 4). The conventions are then evaluated in a simulation study in which the true values are known, so that each convention can be scored against the truth and not merely compared with the others (Section 5), and the comparison is repeated on four real algal growth tests (Section 6). The recommendations and the limitations are given in Sections 7 and 8, and the provenance of each figure quoted is recorded in Section 9.

To run this vignette we will need the following packages.

library(bayesnec)
library(brms)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

2 Toxicity estimates and their reference

2.1 Growth rate and the ErCx notation

In OECD terminology the endpoint is the measured biological response, and OECD Test Guideline 201 (OECD 2026) defines two endpoints from one set of cell counts and requires both to be reported: the average specific growth rate (i.e. the rate constant of population increase) and the yield (i.e. the biomass increase over the test). The r in ErC50 comes from TG 201 and names the endpoint from which the estimate was derived, so that ErC50 is the EC50 for the growth rate and EyC50 is the EC50 for the yield (TG 201 writes this letter as a subscript, whereas we write it inline). For a given dataset EyC50 is systematically lower than ErC50, and the guideline requires the growth rate to be reported because it does not depend on test duration.

An ECx or an NSEC (both defined below) is therefore a toxicity estimate, not an endpoint. This distinction is important here because it is the growth-rate endpoint, and not the toxicity estimate, that can take negative values. Everything below concerns ErCx.

2.2 The ECx reference

bayesnec measures each ECx from the control, which is the predicted mean at the lowest concentration in the supplied predictor, taken per posterior draw. The type argument names what the percentage is measured towards: "absolute" (the default) measures from the control to zero, "relative" from the control to the equation’s lower asymptote, and "range" from the control to the lowest response the curve predicts, whereas "direct" reads the concentration off a nominated response value (see ?ecx for the full definitions).

TG 201 uses the definition given by type = "absolute", under which a 50% effect means the growth rate has been halved relative to the control, and a 100% effect means growth has stopped altogether. This definition has two consequences for a response that can go negative. First, zero growth is 100% effect for any dataset, whatever the control growth rate, so a curve whose lower asymptote is negative descends past 100% effect and continues to decline. Second, effects above 100% are meaningful and are not truncated (ecx_val is not capped), because 120% inhibition of a growth rate is a rate of -0.2 times the control, which is a real measurement on an unbounded response and is the value reported under TG 201.

ErC10 and ErC50 are always located where the curve is above zero, because they require the response to be 90% and 50% of the control respectively, and both of these values are strictly positive. The negative part of the curve can therefore affect these estimates only indirectly, by changing the shape of the fitted curve through the observations at high concentrations, and it is this indirect effect that we quantify in the rest of this vignette.

We do not normalise the response to the control anywhere in this vignette. The absolute ECx already expresses the effect relative to the fitted control response, so dividing the data by the control mean beforehand would apply the same correction twice, and would also distort the error structure (Ritz et al. 2026).

2.3 The NSEC

The NSEC is the no-significant-effect-concentration of Fisher and Fox (2023), i.e. the highest concentration at which the modelled mean response is still statistically indistinguishable from the modelled control response (read up the concentration series, this is the point at which the response first becomes distinguishable from the control). To estimate it, bayesnec takes a lower quantile of the control posterior (by default the 1st percentile, controlled by sig_val) and finds where each posterior draw of the curve crosses it. The NSEC is one of the estimates recommended for guideline derivation under the current Australian and New Zealand technical guidance (Warne et al. 2025), and its relationship to the NEC is described by Fisher et al. (2024).

The NSEC depends on the width of the control posterior, which determines how the results below need to be read. This dependence follows from how the metric is defined, and not from how any approach fits the data. A noisier experiment tends to produce a wider control posterior, and hence a lower reference value and a crossing further to the right, at a higher concentration. Conversely, as the residual error among the control replicates tends to zero, the reference converges on the control mean and the crossing is found at a lower concentration.

Several equations in bayesnec include a nec parameter (a threshold concentration below which the modelled mean response is flat at the control level and above which it declines), so that the curve consists of two straight or curved segments meeting at a corner instead of a single smooth decline. For such an equation the NSEC converges on nec itself as the residual error falls. The true nec is therefore the limiting value of the NSEC, and not its expected value at any finite level of noise.

3 Flooring and the response distribution

Replacing a negative growth rate with zero is more than an edit to the data, because it asserts that the response cannot be negative. This is a statement about the response distribution, and the rest of the analysis then has to be made consistent with it.

However, no available distribution family represents that assertion exactly. A floored response has a point mass at zero, whereas the distributions available for a non-negative continuous response exclude zero itself (a Beta is defined on the open interval (0, 1) and a Gamma on the open interval (0, infinity)). The floored values are therefore outside the support of the family that the flooring implies. A distribution that does represent a continuous non-negative response with a point mass at zero (e.g. a Tweedie) is not available natively in brms.

bayesnec accommodates this by shifting the values inside the support of the Beta or Gamma family. check_data() shifts an exact zero to one tenth of the smallest positive value and, under a Beta, an exact one to 1 - 0.001. bnec() gives one message for each substitution, naming the number of rows, the value substituted and the reason, and, for a substituted zero, the family that would represent a genuine zero instead of shifting it. This accommodation is a device for making an inconsistent specification runnable, and not a model of the response.

Substituting zeros and choosing a bounded family are therefore one practice applied at different stages of the analysis, which is why we do not treat them as alternatives. The floored convention below replaces the negative values and keeps the family unbounded, whereas the beta and gamma conventions make this assertion through the family as well as through the data.

Two cases are outside this argument. A row whose value was never recorded, because the population fell below a counting limit, is a censored observation and not a floored one, and is exempt from the substitution. A response that is genuinely zero because the population died is a different process again, for which the hurdle and zero-inflated families are designed (see the Hurdle and zero-inflated concentration-response models vignette). However, these families are not a remedy for a substituted negative.

4 Zero-asymptote equations under a Gaussian family

The interval within which a response distribution allows the mean to fall is a property of the distribution, and not of the link function. The mean of a Gaussian distribution is unconstrained, because the data enter the likelihood only through the residual, and a negative fitted mean is therefore an ordinary prediction and not an invalid one.

For this reason the six declining equations whose lower asymptote is fixed at zero (nec3param, ecxexp, ecxsigm, ecxwb1p3, ecxwb2p3 and ecxll3) are retained under a Gaussian family, although none of them can predict a negative mean while top is positive. An absolute ECx is reported for each of them, even though none has a bot parameter. Under a Gaussian family the declining candidate set that bnec() fits by default includes these six and the eight other declining equations and, together with the constant equation ecxflat (which is also in the "decline" group), consists of fifteen equations.

models()$decline
#>  [1] "nec3param" "nec4param" "neclin"    "ecxlin"    "ecxexp"    "ecxsigm"   "ecx4param" "ecxwb1"    "ecxwb2"   
#> [10] "ecxwb1p3"  "ecxwb2p3"  "ecxll5"    "ecxll4"    "ecxll3"    "ecxflat"

In practice, this means that the curve shape described for algal growth-rate data by both TG 201 and Ritz et al. (2026) (a lower asymptote fixed at zero, representing complete inhibition) can be fitted directly to the measurements as recorded, and can be weighed against the shapes with a free lower asymptote by the same model averaging that bayesnec applies to everything else. Whether that shape is used then depends on the weight the data give it, and not on a choice made in the model specification. The decision to replace the measurements is a separate one, made before any equation is fitted, and it is this decision that we examine in the remaining sections.

5 Simulation study

Real datasets can show that the conventions disagree, but not which of them is correct, because the true toxicity of a real substance is unknown. We therefore make the comparison on simulated data, for which the true ErC10, ErC50 and nec are known by construction, so that each convention can be scored against them.

5.1 The conventions compared

We compare six conventions, which differ only in what is done to the data before fitting and in the response distribution that is then used.

name what the analyst does
measured use the growth rates as recorded
censored declare each negative value left-censored at zero
deleted delete the rows holding a negative value
floored replace each negative value with zero
beta floor, scale the response to (0, 1], fit a Beta
gamma floor, fit a Gamma

Each convention then calls bnec() with the package defaults, i.e. the default priors derived from its own prepared data, the default declining candidate set for its family, and the default model averaging over that set (pseudo-BMA with a Bayesian bootstrap, which bnec() uses when loo_controls is not supplied). No convention is given a prior or an equation chosen by another convention. The difference between two conventions is therefore the difference a practitioner would obtain by following each convention through, and not a contrast in the likelihood only, with everything else held artificially fixed.

If the equation were held fixed (e.g. at nec4param), any difference could be attributed only to the treatment of the data. However, this answers a question about the likelihood, and not the question a reader has, which is what happens to the number they will report. A fixed equation would also introduce an artefact, because on altered data a fixed nec4param is no longer the equation that generated them, and part of what it measured would then be misspecification that the convention did not cause.

The measured convention uses the growth rates as recorded, with the lower asymptote left free wherever the equation has one, and provides the reference for all of the results below.

bnec(y ~ crf(x, "decline"), data = dat, family = gaussian(link = "identity"))

The censored convention declares each negative value censored at zero, so that the model is told the observation is at or below zero without being told its value. This is the option available when the negative values were never recorded. Censoring also changes which observations constrain the mean most strongly, because a censored row contributes the probability that the response is at or below the bound, and not a density (see the Censoring section of the Single model usage vignette).

dat_censored <- dat |>
  mutate(cens = ifelse(y < 0, "left", "none"),
         y = ifelse(y < 0, 0, y))
bnec(y | cens(cens) ~ crf(x, "decline"), data = dat_censored,
     family = gaussian(link = "identity"))

The deleted convention drops the rows holding a negative value and analyses the remaining data unchanged. Nothing false is asserted about any observation that is kept. However, the replication per concentration can change, and a whole treatment group may disappear at the top of the series (i.e. at the highest concentrations).

bnec(y ~ crf(x, "decline"), data = filter(dat, y >= 0),
     family = gaussian(link = "identity"))

The floored convention replaces each negative growth rate with zero and does not change the model.

dat_floored <- mutate(dat, y = pmax(y, 0))
bnec(y ~ crf(x, "decline"), data = dat_floored,
     family = gaussian(link = "identity"))

The beta convention divides the floored response by its maximum, so that it is in the interval (0, 1], and fits a Beta. Dividing by the maximum is how these data have been prepared in the work this vignette draws on, whereas dividing by the control mean is at least as common elsewhere, and Ritz et al. (2026) set out why the response should not be divided by either before fitting.

dat_beta <- dat |>
  mutate(y = pmax(y, 0)) |>
  mutate(y = y / max(y))
bnec(y ~ crf(x, "decline"), data = dat_beta, family = Beta(link = "identity"))

The gamma convention applies no scaling, and fits a Gamma to the floored response.

bnec(y ~ crf(x, "decline"), data = dat_floored,
     family = Gamma(link = "identity"))

Under the beta and gamma conventions the zeros created by flooring are shifted off the boundary by check_data() (Section 3), and this shift is part of the convention under test, not something the study pre-empts. Dividing by the maximum does not affect the reported toxicity estimates, because ecx(type = "absolute") solves f(x) = control * (1 - x/100). A positive scaling of the response therefore applies to both sides of this equation, and the concentration at which the curve meets the target is unchanged. The choice of family changes the fitted curve, but not the definition of the estimate.

The candidate set differs between families, because the declining set is filtered according to what the support of each family allows. Under a Gaussian family the study used the fourteen equations listed in Section 4 other than ecxflat (which was added to the set after the study was run), whereas under a Beta and under a Gamma it used twelve.

5.2 Design

The data are generated from nec4param, which is in the candidate set of each Gaussian convention, so that the generating shape is available to be recovered and the weight it receives is itself informative.

nec4param_curve <- function(x, top, bot, beta, nec) {
  bot + (top - bot) * exp(-exp(beta) * (x - nec) * (x >= nec))
}

The truth is parameterised so that the two experimental factors are explicit. The control growth rate is set by the control fold-change R (the factor by which the control population multiplies over a test of length t), and the depth of the lower asymptote is set as a multiple delta of that control rate. For example, at delta = 2 the population declines twice as fast at the highest concentrations as it grows in the control. The three levels used (delta = 2, 4 and 8) span the range measured on the real datasets.

sim_truth <- function(R = 2.3, delta = 4, t = 7, nec = 1.3, beta = -3.573) {
  mu_0 <- log(R) / t                    # true control growth rate
  bot <- -delta * mu_0                  # lower asymptote, delta x deeper than top
  list(R = R, delta = delta, t = t, top = mu_0, bot = bot,
       beta = beta, nec = nec,
       # where the true curve crosses zero growth
       zero_crossing = nec + log((1 + delta) / delta) / exp(beta))
}

The design is a geometric concentration series spanning a factor of one hundred, with ten controls and five replicates at each of twelve concentrations (n = 70), matching the real designs. The position of the highest concentration is the second factor, and is expressed as a multiple top_factor of the concentration at which the true curve crosses zero. At top_factor = 1.0 the series stops exactly at the crossing and about one design point in fourteen has a non-positive true mean, whereas at 2.0 the series extends well past the crossing and one design point in seven has a non-positive true mean. This factor therefore determines how much negative data there is for a convention to act on.

sim_design <- function(truth, top_factor = 1, n_conc = 12, n_rep = 5,
                       n_control = 10, span = 100) {
  x_max <- top_factor * truth$zero_crossing
  concs <- exp(seq(log(x_max / span), log(x_max), length.out = n_conc))
  data.frame(x = c(rep(0, n_control), rep(concs, each = n_rep)))
}

The residual scale is constant along the curve, and the fits are homoscedastic to match, so that no convention is misspecified in its variance and only the mean structure is under test. When the within-dose standard deviation of the alga data is measured against position on the curve (with substituted rows excluded), only one of the four datasets shows a gradient at all (c_proliferum, fitted ratio 14.1, slope p < 0.001), whereas the ratios for the other three are 1.2 to 1.5 (p > 0.35). Generating all cells as heteroscedastic would therefore assert as general a pattern seen in one dataset. It would also misspecify each convention identically, which is a confound shared by the whole comparison and not a feature of it.

sim_sigma <- function(x, truth, sigma_0_abs) rep(sigma_0_abs, length(x))

simulate_dataset <- function(truth, design, sigma_0_abs, seed = NULL) {
  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)
  mu <- nec4param_curve(design$x, truth$top, truth$bot, truth$beta, truth$nec)
  data.frame(x = design$x,
             y = rnorm(length(mu), mu, sim_sigma(design$x, truth, sigma_0_abs)))
}

The control residual standard deviation is held at a fixed absolute value, anchored so that it corresponds to a coefficient of variation of 9.6% at R = 2.3, rather than at a fixed coefficient of variation. Under a fixed coefficient of variation the generating model is exactly scale-equivariant in the growth rate, so changing R would change nothing that is reported. Holding the absolute error fixed instead means that increasing R increases the signal but does not change the noise, which makes R an axis of measurement precision.

sigma_0_abs <- 0.096 * log(2.3) / 7   # absolute control SD, anchored at R = 2.3

The design consists of seven cells. Four of them (p1 to p4) have delta = 4 and top_factor = 2.0 and increasing values of R, giving four levels of measurement precision with an otherwise identical design and truth. Two more (d2 and d8) change how far the true curve descends below zero, and the seventh (ctl) stops the concentration series at the zero crossing, so that the conventions have almost nothing to act on. Each cell was simulated 100 times and each simulated dataset was analysed under all six conventions, giving 7 x 100 x 6 = 4,200 model-averaged fits and 52,533 individual equation fits. Sampling used four chains of 4,000 iterations with 2,000 warmup, adapt_delta = 0.99 and max_treedepth = 12. All fits are retained in the summaries, as no unit failed and no estimate was unidentified.

cells <- data.frame(
  cell = c("p1", "p2", "p3", "p4", "d2", "d8", "ctl"),
  delta = c(4, 4, 4, 4, 2, 8, 4),
  top_factor = c(2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1),
  R = c(2.3, 3.3, 17, 73, 2.3, 2.3, 2.3)
)

cell_detail <- function(s) {
  tr <- sim_truth(R = s$R, delta = s$delta)
  dz <- sim_design(tr, top_factor = s$top_factor)
  mu <- nec4param_curve(dz$x, tr$top, tr$bot, tr$beta, tr$nec)
  true_ecx <- function(p) {
    target <- tr$top * (1 - p / 100)
    tr$nec + log((tr$top - tr$bot) / (target - tr$bot)) / exp(tr$beta)
  }
  data.frame(top = tr$top, bot = tr$bot, x_max = max(dz$x),
             ErC10 = true_ecx(10), ErC50 = true_ecx(50),
             cv_control = sigma_0_abs / tr$top,
             # tolerance, not `<= 0`: at top_factor = 1 the highest design point
             # sits exactly on the crossing, so a strict test flips on floating
             # point and reports 0 for some cells and 1/14 for others
             prop_negative = mean(mu <= 1e-10))
}
cells <- cbind(cells, do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(cells)),
                                            function(i) cell_detail(cells[i, ]))))
Table 1. The seven simulated cells. top and bot are the true upper and lower asymptotes of the growth rate; prop. negative is the proportion of the 70 design points whose true mean growth rate is at or below zero. The true nec is 1.3 in every cell.
Cell delta top factor R top bot max conc. true ErC10 true ErC50 control CV prop. negative
p1 4 2 2.3 0.119 -0.476 18.5 2.02 5.05 0.096 0.143
p2 4 2 3.3 0.171 -0.682 18.5 2.02 5.05 0.067 0.143
p3 4 2 17.0 0.405 -1.619 18.5 2.02 5.05 0.028 0.143
p4 4 2 73.0 0.613 -2.452 18.5 2.02 5.05 0.019 0.143
d2 2 2 2.3 0.119 -0.238 31.5 2.51 7.79 0.096 0.143
d8 8 2 2.3 0.119 -0.952 11.0 1.70 3.34 0.096 0.143
ctl 4 1 2.3 0.119 -0.476 9.2 2.02 5.05 0.096 0.071

Three features of Table 1 are important for interpreting the results below. First, the true ErC10 and ErC50 depend only on delta, so p1 to p4 share one estimand and differ only in how precisely it can be measured. Second, the proportion of negative true means is one in seven in all cells except ctl, where it is one in fourteen, which in the realised datasets corresponds to about 10 negative observations out of 70 (against about 2 in ctl). Third, the control coefficient of variation falls from 9.6% to 1.9% across p1 to p4, and this is the precision sweep on which the rest of this section is built.

Figure 1 shows one simulated dataset from each cell. The scatter of the observations relative to the range of the true curve narrows from p1 to p4, and in each cell except ctl the true curve is below zero growth at the highest two concentrations, whereas in ctl the series ends where the true curve crosses zero.

curve_data <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(cells)), function(i) {
  s <- cells[i, ]
  tr <- sim_truth(R = s$R, delta = s$delta)
  xx <- seq(0, s$x_max, length.out = 300)
  data.frame(cell = s$cell, x = xx,
             mu = nec4param_curve(xx, tr$top, tr$bot, tr$beta, tr$nec))
}))

point_data <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(cells)), function(i) {
  s <- cells[i, ]
  tr <- sim_truth(R = s$R, delta = s$delta)
  d <- simulate_dataset(tr, sim_design(tr, s$top_factor), sigma_0_abs,
                        seed = 42 + i)
  data.frame(cell = s$cell, d)
}))

# Panels in design order -- the precision sweep first, then the cells that change
# the truth or the design -- rather than alphabetically.
cell_levels <- c("p1", "p2", "p3", "p4", "d2", "d8", "ctl")
cells$cell <- factor(cells$cell, levels = cell_levels)
curve_data$cell <- factor(curve_data$cell, levels = cell_levels)
point_data$cell <- factor(point_data$cell, levels = cell_levels)

lab <- setNames(
  sprintf("%s:  delta %g,  top %.1f,  R %.1f\n(control CV %.1f%%)",
          cells$cell, cells$delta, cells$top_factor, cells$R,
          100 * cells$cv_control),
  levels(cells$cell))

# controls sit at x = 0 and have no position on a log axis, so they are dropped
# from this figure; every fit uses them
ggplot(subset(point_data, x > 0), aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(data = cells, aes(xintercept = ErC10),
             linetype = "dotted", colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(data = cells, aes(xintercept = ErC50),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = subset(curve_data, x > 0), aes(y = mu), linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ cell, scales = "free", ncol = 4,
             labeller = labeller(cell = lab)) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Concentration (log scale)",
       y = expression("Specific growth rate ("*d^-1*")")) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 8) +
  theme(panel.spacing = unit(0.35, "lines"),
        plot.margin = margin(2, 4, 2, 2),
        strip.background = element_blank(), strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0))

Figure 1. The seven simulated cells. Points are one simulated dataset per cell; the solid line is the true curve; the dashed horizontal line is zero growth. Vertical lines mark the true ErC10 (dotted) and ErC50 (dashed). Panels are labelled with the cell name, its design factors and the control coefficient of variation it realises.

5.3 One dataset under each convention

The tables and figures below summarise each cell over its 100 realisations, and such a summary does not show what a convention does to an individual dataset. We therefore also fitted all six conventions to a single simulated dataset from p1, the noisiest cell tested, in which 10 of the seventy design points have a true mean growth rate at or below zero and 11 of the seventy simulated observations were negative (Figure 2). This realisation is the one drawn for the p1 exemplar by a seed fixed on the cell and convention names, so it was chosen before any result was seen and not selected afterwards for the picture it makes.

ggplot(panel_fit, aes(x = x)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = panel_cell$ErC50, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey60") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = arm), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_point(data = subset(panel_points, x > 0),
             aes(y = y, shape = altered), size = 1.1, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = panel_true, aes(y = y), linewidth = 1, colour = "grey10") +
  geom_line(aes(y = y, colour = arm), linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 16, `TRUE` = 1), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = arm_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = arm_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ arm, ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = "Concentration (log scale)",
       y = expression("Specific growth rate ("*d^-1*")")) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 9) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0))

Figure 2. One simulated dataset from cell p1, fitted under each of the six conventions. Points are the data each convention was given; open symbols mark the 11 observations it altered or dropped, drawn at zero by the four conventions that substitute and at their measured values under deleted, which discards those rows. measured alters none, so nothing in its panel is marked. The coloured line is the model-averaged posterior median and the band its 95% credible interval; the black line is the true curve. The dashed horizontal line is zero growth and the dashed vertical line the true ErC50. The controls sit at a concentration of zero and have no position on a log axis, so they are not drawn; every fit uses them.

Under measured the model-averaged curve follows the true curve along its whole length, including the part below zero, and its credible band is narrow throughout (Figure 2). Under censored the median also follows the true curve, although the band widens once the curve passes zero, because a row declared to be below a bound provides less information about where the curve goes than a measurement does.

In contrast, the three conventions that put a zero in place of the measurement (floored, beta and gamma) produce a curve that flattens onto zero instead of continuing to decline. This flattening appears from a little below the true ErC50 (the dashed vertical line), and therefore begins at lower concentrations than the substituted rows themselves. This is likely to be the mechanism behind the biases reported below: the substitution is made at the top of the concentration series, but the resulting curve is displaced over a range that includes the concentrations from which the estimates are read. The displacement is small at the ErC50 and large at the low-concentration end of the curve, where the NSEC is read, and this ordering is measured in Sections 5.4 and 5.6.

The deleted panel shows a different consequence. In this dataset, removing all rows with a negative value removed the highest concentrations entirely, so the fitted curve stops where the surviving data stop, and the design is no longer the one that was run.

The gamma panel shows a failure of the variance and not of the mean. Its credible band is widest at the control (on the left of the panel), where the generated residual spread is no wider than at any other concentration, because an identity-link Gamma ties the spread to the fitted mean. We quantify this with a posterior predictive check in Section 5.4.

5.4 ErC10 and ErC50

Relative bias is the mean of the estimated value minus the true value over the 100 realisations of a cell, expressed as a percentage of the true value. The precision sweep is the most informative comparison in the study, because it distinguishes the two sources of error in an estimate: estimation error shrinks as an experiment becomes more precise, whereas the error due to model misspecification does not.

bias_plot <- function(d, ests) {
  ggplot(subset(d, estimate %in% ests),
         aes(x = cv_f, y = rel_bias, colour = arm, group = arm)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_point(size = 1.8) +
    # One label per series at the right-hand edge rather than a key: the label
    # sits on the line it names, which is the secondary encoding the palette
    # note above depends on.
    scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.4, 0.4))) +
    facet_grid(estimate ~ handling, scales = "free_y") +
    labs(x = "Control coefficient of variation (%)  —  more precise →",
         y = "Relative bias in the estimate (%)") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = arm_cols, breaks = arm_levels) +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 9) +
    theme(strip.background = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom",
          legend.title = element_blank(), legend.key.width = unit(1.4, "lines"))
}
bias_plot(precision, c("ErC10", "ErC50"))

Figure 3. Relative bias in the estimated ErC10 and ErC50 against the control coefficient of variation, which decreases to the right as the experiment becomes more precise. Each point summarises 100 simulated datasets. The dashed line is zero bias.

The three conventions that retain the measurement converge on the true ErC50 (Figure 3). Across p1 to p4 the bias of measured ranges from -0.4% to -0.2%, that of censored from -0.7% to -0.2%, and that of deleted from -2.4% to 0.0%, so that all three are within half a per cent of the truth at the highest precision tested.

In contrast, flooring does not converge. The magnitude of the ErC50 bias of floored falls from -3.4% to -2.3% and then stops falling, and that of beta remains between -4.4% and -5.8% throughout, so both conventions make the substance appear more toxic than it is. This residual bias is smaller than the 8 to 15% reported for these conventions under a fixed nec4param, because the candidate set contains the zero-asymptote shapes that floored data resemble (Section 4), and averaging over these shapes absorbs part of the distortion. However, it does not absorb all of it.

The Gamma converges on the true ErC50, but is the least accurate of the six conventions on ErC10. Its ErC50 bias falls from 4.3% to 0.2% across the sweep, whereas its ErC10 is displaced by -8.7% at the noisiest and -25.0% at the most precise. This bias increases as the experiment becomes more precise, which indicates misspecification and not estimation error.

The cause is in the variance and not in the mean, as a posterior predictive check shows. These data are generated with a residual standard deviation that is constant along the curve, so what a correctly specified family should predict is known exactly (i.e. the generated value at each concentration). Each fit of the four precision cells was refitted, and its model-averaged predicted spread was compared with the generated one, for 100 realisations per cell and convention. We summarise the comparison by the control ratio (the predicted spread at the lowest concentration divided by the generated value) and the gradient (the ratio of the predicted spread at the control to that at the highest concentration), both of which should therefore be one for a correctly specified family.

Because measured is correctly specified by construction, its values are the closest this statistic comes to one on these data, and provide the reference against which the other conventions are read: a control ratio of 1.00 to 0.98, with 95% of realisations between 0.81 and 1.18, and a gradient of 1.03.

An identity-link Gamma cannot reproduce a constant spread, because it ties the residual standard deviation to the mean. It overstates the spread at the control by a factor of 2.51 to 2.69, and its gradient ranges from 181 at the noisiest cell to 90 at the most precise, against a true value of one. The floored block of observations is therefore given almost all of the weight in the likelihood and the control scatter almost none, so that it is the fit at the shoulder of the curve (where a 10% decline is read, i.e. the ErC10) that is distorted.

This check also shows what flooring does and does not damage. Under a Gaussian family the floored data are described by a correctly specified variance model, with a control ratio for floored of 0.91 to 1.12 and a gradient of 1.04, both within the reference. What the substitution changes is the mean structure (examined in Section 5.7), whereas under a Gamma the failures of the mean and of the variance compound.

The Beta is a third case. Its control ratio of 1.09 to 1.10 is within the reference, and its gradient of 1.71 to 2.66 is a mild departure compared with that of the Gamma. Whatever displaces the ErC10 of the Beta is therefore not the variance model.

At the highest precision tested, the intervals of gamma are 2.14 times as wide as those of measured on ErC50, which keeps its ErC50 coverage nominal while its point estimate for ErC10 is a quarter low.

The Beta is displaced in the other direction on ErC10, from -0.9% at the noisiest to 9.3% at the most precise. This bias also increases as the experiment becomes more precise, which again indicates misspecification and not estimation error.

ggplot(design_cells, aes(x = rel_bias, y = arm, colour = arm)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  # estimate on the columns, not the rows: facet_grid frees a scale per column,
  # and the three estimates are on scales that differ by an order of magnitude,
  # so sharing one x axis across them would hide everything but the NSEC.
  facet_grid(cell ~ estimate, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(arm_levels)) +
  labs(x = "Relative bias in the estimate (%)", y = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = arm_cols, guide = "none") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 9) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(), legend.position = "none")

Figure 4. Relative bias in the three cells that change the truth or the design rather than the measurement precision, all at a control coefficient of variation of 9.6%. d2 and d8 change how far the true curve descends below zero; ctl stops the concentration series at the zero crossing, leaving about two negative observations in seventy for a convention to act on.

The depth to which the curve descends below zero changes the size of the effect, but not its direction (Figure 4). Between d2 and d8 the ErC50 bias of floored is -4.0% and -2.0%, and that of beta -5.0% and -3.1%, against 0.0% and 1.1% for measured.

The ctl cell is the one that indicates whether any of this applies to a reader’s own data. Its concentration series stops at the zero crossing, so a realised dataset contains about two negative observations instead of ten, and the four Gaussian conventions then span 0.4 percentage points of ErC50 bias between them. This compares with 3.0 in p1, which has equal control variability and four times as many negative observations. Where essentially none of the observations are at or below zero growth, the choice of convention is therefore unlikely to change the reported value.

5.5 Credible interval coverage

Coverage is the proportion of the 100 realisations whose 95% credible interval contains the true value. We report it together with the mean interval width, because a wide interval and an accurate one both achieve nominal coverage, although they are different results.

cov_plot <- function(d, ests) {
  ggplot(subset(d, estimate %in% ests),
         aes(x = cv_f, y = coverage, colour = arm, group = arm)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_point(size = 1.8) +
    scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.4, 0.4))) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
    facet_grid(estimate ~ handling) +
    labs(x = "Control coefficient of variation (%)  —  more precise →",
         y = "Proportion of 95% intervals containing the truth") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = arm_cols, breaks = arm_levels) +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 9) +
    theme(strip.background = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom",
          legend.title = element_blank(), legend.key.width = unit(1.4, "lines"))
}
cov_plot(precision, c("ErC10", "ErC50"))

Figure 5. Proportion of 95% credible intervals containing the true ErC10 or ErC50, against the control coefficient of variation. The dashed line is nominal coverage.

The three conventions that retain the measurement maintain nominal coverage across the sweep (Figure 5). At the highest precision the interval of measured contains the true ErC50 in 0.97 of the 100 realisations, compared with 0.99 for censored and 0.99 for deleted.

In contrast, the coverage of floored falls as the experiment becomes more precise, from 0.85 to 0.24 on ErC50, and that of beta from 0.99 to 0.52. This is the practical consequence of a bias that does not converge, because the interval narrows around a centre that remains displaced. A laboratory that improves its technique, adds replicates and reduces its control variability is therefore likely, if it floors its negative values, to produce an analysis that is more confident and no less wrong. The ErC10 of gamma shows this failure more severely, with coverage falling from 0.84 to 0.01.

Without the interval width, these coverage results could be read the wrong way round. At the highest precision floored has an ErC50 interval 1.47 times as wide as that of measured and contains the truth in a quarter of the realisations, whereas gamma has an interval 2.14 times as wide and contains the truth at the nominal rate. Neither coverage nor width should therefore be reported without the other.

5.6 The NSEC

ErC10 and the NSEC are both commonly used as a no-effect value, but the conventions affect them differently. Because the true nec is the limiting value of the NSEC as the residual error goes to zero, and not its expected value at any finite level of noise (Section 2.3), an approach is identified by the precision sweep and not by any single cell. A correctly specified approach remains on the truth as the experiment becomes more precise, whereas a misspecified one departs further from it the more precise the experiment becomes.

# Bias and coverage in one figure, as two rows of a facet rather than two plots
# stacked by a layout package: the reference line differs between the rows, so
# it is supplied as data rather than as a constant.
nsec_long <- subset(precision, estimate == "NSEC") |>
  select(arm, handling, cv_f, `Relative bias (%)` = rel_bias,
         `Interval coverage` = coverage) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Relative bias (%)`, `Interval coverage`),
               names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(metric = factor(metric, levels = c("Relative bias (%)",
                                            "Interval coverage")))
nsec_ref <- data.frame(metric = factor(c("Relative bias (%)",
                                         "Interval coverage"),
                                       levels = levels(nsec_long$metric)),
                       yint = c(0, 0.95))

ggplot(nsec_long, aes(x = cv_f, y = value, colour = arm, group = arm)) +
  geom_hline(data = nsec_ref, aes(yintercept = yint),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.4, 0.4))) +
  facet_grid(metric ~ handling, scales = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  labs(x = "Control coefficient of variation (%)  —  more precise \u2192",
       y = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = arm_cols, breaks = arm_levels) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 9) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(), strip.placement = "outside",
        legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.key.width = unit(1.4, "lines"))

Figure 6. Relative bias in the estimated NSEC against the true nec of 1.3 (upper row) and the proportion of 95% credible intervals containing it (lower row), against the control coefficient of variation. The dashed lines are zero bias and nominal coverage. A correctly specified approach stays on zero bias as the residual error falls; a misspecified one departs further the more precise the experiment becomes.

The retaining conventions remain near the true nec across the sweep, with no trend in either direction (Figure 6). At the highest precision the NSEC bias of measured is 3.2%, that of censored 2.4% and that of deleted 0.7%. These biases are not constant across the sweep (the largest single departure of the three is 10.8%, for measured at a control coefficient of variation of 6.7%), but the departures do not grow as the experiment becomes more precise, and this is what distinguishes estimation error from misspecification.

Section 2.3 gives the reason to expect an overestimate at finite noise. Under the priors used here, however, this overshoot is small enough to be lost in the Monte Carlo error of 100 realisations, and does not appear as a trend. It was visible under the superseded prior, where these three conventions ranged from about +14% down to +4%. A correctly specified approach is therefore identified here by remaining on the truth as the residual error falls, and not by the direction from which it approaches.

In contrast, the conventions that replace the measurement diverge downward. The NSEC bias of floored ranges from -11.9% to -52.9%, that of beta from -1.4% to -42.7%, and that of gamma from 25.0% to -71.6%. Coverage follows this pattern: at the highest precision the interval of floored contains the true nec in 0.00 of the 100 realisations and that of gamma in 0.04, against 0.97 for censored and 0.98 for deleted.

For a convention that floors, the errors in ErC50 and in the NSEC are in the same direction. Such a convention returns an ErC50 and an NSEC that are both too low, so the substance appears more toxic than it is on both estimates, which for a guideline value is the cautious direction in which to be wrong. However, being cautious is different from being correct. At the highest precision tested the NSEC of floored is displaced by more than half the true value, which is an error comparable in size to the estimate, and its interval contains the truth in none of the 100 realisations. An estimate that provides no information about the quantity it names cannot be relied on to be cautious on the next dataset either.

measured is the only convention whose NSEC coverage falls without its bias diverging, from 0.99 to 0.88. This is the property of the metric described in Section 2.3, and not a failure of the convention. The NSEC overshoots the true nec slightly at finite noise, and by p4 the interval has narrowed faster than the remaining bias of 3.2% has closed, so that an interval correctly placed to within a few per cent no longer contains the truth. Over this range censored and deleted maintain nominal coverage, with intervals 1.81 and 2.10 times as wide.

5.7 The equations the data are made to resemble

Each convention is model-averaged over the declining set for its family, and the data were generated from nec4param, so the weight each convention gives to nec4param measures how closely the data, once the convention has been applied, still resemble the process that produced them. This weight describes the data supplied to the fit and not the substance, and we report it because it explains the biases above.

Table 2. Mean model weight on the generating equation nec4param across the precision sweep, averaged over 100 realisations per cell. The remaining weight is spread over the other eleven to thirteen equations in the candidate set.
Convention p1 (CV 9.6%) p2 (CV 6.7%) p3 (CV 2.8%) p4 (CV 1.9%)
measured 0.506 0.714 0.849 0.852
censored 0.300 0.355 0.344 0.469
deleted 0.111 0.191 0.254 0.363
floored 0.066 0.061 0.003 0.000
beta 0.066 0.050 0.017 0.010
gamma 0.036 0.021 0.000 0.000

Given the measurements as recorded, model averaging identifies the generating equation, and does so more clearly as the experiment becomes more precise (Table 2): nec4param receives 0.51 of the weight at a control coefficient of variation of 9.6% and 0.85 at 1.9%. Under censored and deleted it still receives 0.47 and 0.36 of the weight at the highest precision, with most of the remainder given to neclin, which shares its breakpoint and differs only in the shape below it.

In contrast, under the conventions that replace the measurement the generating equation receives essentially none of the weight, which goes instead to a zero-asymptote shape. At the highest precision floored gives nec4param 0.00 of the weight and ecxsigm 0.96, whereas gamma gives ecxwb1 0.92. Both of these equations decay smoothly to zero, which is what floored data look like, and the weights favour them more strongly the more precise the experiment. A model weight is evidence about which shape fits the data supplied, and not about which process produced the measurements, and on floored data these are different questions.

The six equations whose lower asymptote is fixed at zero provide the clearest signature of the substitution, although they identify it only where the substitution itself imposes the boundary. At the highest precision these equations receive 0.98 of the weight under floored, against 0.00 under measured and 0.00 under censored. Under beta and gamma they receive only 0.04 and 0.00, because these families already exclude a negative mean, and an equation with a free lower asymptote is bounded below in any case. The weight on these six equations is therefore a diagnostic for flooring under an unbounded family, and not for the zero boundary in general.

6 Worked case studies

The simulation establishes which conventions recover the truth, but it cannot show how large the difference is on a real dataset, where the truth is unknown and the design, the noise and the shape of the response are not under the analyst’s control. We therefore analysed four marine microalgal growth tests under all six conventions, and compared each estimate with the measured estimate on that dataset.

The four tests are included in bayesnec as the alga data. Two are tests on Cladocopium proliferum (a coral endosymbiont) over seven days, and two are on Rhodomonas salina over three days, with each species exposed to two contaminants on undisclosed and mutually incomparable concentration scales. The summary of the datasets in Table 3 is computed from the data that ship with the package, so it describes whichever version you have installed.

data(alga)

# The four case studies are the four species-by-contaminant cells of `alga`.
# The names used throughout this section are the vignette's; the mapping is by
# cell rather than by row order, so it survives any reordering of the data.
alga$dataset <- factor(
  paste0(as.character(alga$species), ifelse(alga$contaminant == "B", "2", "")),
  levels = c("c_proliferum", "c_proliferum2", "r_salina", "r_salina2"))

# The growth rate implied by the counting limit of 10 cells per mL, against the
# starting density recorded for the test. Where the source substituted a zero
# for a below-limit count -- flagged `sgr_source == "substituted"` -- this is the
# rate the substitution implies, and it is what the retaining conventions use in
# place of the substituted zero.
alga$below_limit <- alga$sgr_source == "substituted"
alga$limit_rate <- (log(10) - log(alga$density_initial)) / alga$days
alga$y <- ifelse(alga$below_limit, alga$limit_rate, alga$sgr)

datasets <- alga |>
  group_by(dataset, species, duration_d = days) |>
  summarise(n = n(), n_conc = n_distinct(dose),
            control_rate = mean(y[dose == 0]),
            below_limit = sum(below_limit),
            n_negative = sum(y < 0),
            prop_at_or_below_zero = mean(y <= 0), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(fold_change_R = exp(control_rate * duration_d), .before = below_limit)
Table 3. The four case-study datasets, computed from the alga data that ship with the package. Below limit counts the rows whose population fell below the counting limit, for which the source substituted a zero. All four have a substantial proportion of observations at or below zero growth, so all four are in the regime where Section 5 applies.
c_proliferum c_proliferum2 r_salina r_salina2
Species c_proliferum c_proliferum r_salina r_salina
Days 7 7 3 3
n 85 70 85 70
Concentrations 14 13 14 13
Control rate (per d) 0.119 0.169 1.431 0.951
Fold change R 2.3 3.3 73.1 17.3
Below limit 0 0 16 4
Negative 12 10 20 21
Prop. at or below zero 0.14 0.14 0.24 0.30

6.1 Undefined growth rates in the Rhodomonas tests

At the highest concentrations in both Rhodomonas tests the population fell below the counting limit of 10 cells per mL, so the density is recorded as zero and the specific growth rate is undefined, not negative. These rows are flagged sgr_source == "substituted" in alga (16 on r_salina and 4 on r_salina2, Table 3). The Cladocopium tests have no such rows, and their negative values are measurements.

Because there is no measured value to retain in these rows, each convention must substitute something. The measured convention uses the growth rate implied by the counting limit, which is itself a substitution, so on these two datasets it is not a true analysis of the measurements, and the comparison is correspondingly weaker. This situation is likely to be common with real algal data, and is one of the reasons left-censoring is useful, as it can express “at or below the limit” without inventing a value.

The undefined rows also determine what censored means on these two datasets. Left-censoring declares that the true value is at or below a bound, so the bound should be the tightest one the measurement supports. This is zero for a growth rate that was measured and was negative, but the counting limit itself for a row that fell below it. The latter is a stronger statement than “below zero”, and is the one thing the test does establish about that row.

6.2 Estimates from each convention

Each dataset is prepared by each convention exactly as in Section 5.1, and passed to bnec() with package defaults, so the conventions and candidate sets in the case studies match those in the simulation.

# Every convention takes bnec()'s own default priors here, unlike the
# simulation, where one prior is fixed per cell and convention so that repeated
# realisations compile one Stan program rather than a hundred. Each dataset is
# fitted once, so there is nothing for a fixed prior to save, and taking the
# defaults is the practice under examination.
fit_case <- function(d, convention) {
  d$y <- ifelse(d$below_limit, d$limit_rate, d$sgr)
  gauss <- gaussian(link = "identity")
  switch(convention,
    measured = bnec(y ~ crf(dose, "decline"), data = d, family = gauss),
    floored  = bnec(y ~ crf(dose, "decline"), data = transform(d, y = pmax(y, 0)),
                    family = gauss),
    deleted  = bnec(y ~ crf(dose, "decline"), data = d[d$y >= 0, ],
                    family = gauss),
    # Zero for a measured negative; the counting limit for a row that fell below
    # it, which is what the test actually establishes about that row.
    censored = bnec(y | cens(cens) ~ crf(dose, "decline"),
                    data = transform(d,
                      cens = ifelse(below_limit | y < 0, "left", "none"),
                      y = ifelse(below_limit, limit_rate, pmax(y, 0))),
                    family = gauss),
    beta     = bnec(y ~ crf(dose, "decline"),
                    data = transform(d, y = pmax(y, 0) / max(pmax(y, 0))),
                    family = Beta(link = "identity")),
    gamma    = bnec(y ~ crf(dose, "decline"), data = transform(d, y = pmax(y, 0)),
                    family = Gamma(link = "identity")))
}

These 24 fits are not run when this vignette is built. Instead, they are run in the compendium used for the simulation, against the pinned version of bayesnec used there, and their results are transcribed here (Section 9 gives the time they take and what this means for reading them).

Because the toxicity values of the four datasets are on completely different concentration scales, each estimate is shown as a ratio, i.e. the estimate from a convention divided by the measured estimate on that dataset, so that a ratio of 1 is exact agreement (Figure 7).

# Clipping by pmax/pmin on the data rather than a scale limit, to avoid
# depending on `scales` for an out-of-bounds handler. An interval that runs past
# the panel is already flagged unusable and is drawn with an open symbol.
ratio_lim <- c(0.1, 4)
case_ratios$rlo_p <- pmax(case_ratios$rlo, ratio_lim[1])
case_ratios$rhi_p <- pmin(case_ratios$rhi, ratio_lim[2])

ggplot(case_ratios, aes(x = r, y = arm, colour = arm, shape = usable)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = rlo_p, xmax = rhi_p), orientation = "y",
                width = 0, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, fill = "white") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("TRUE" = 16, "FALSE" = 21), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(arm_levels)) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4), limits = ratio_lim) +
  facet_grid(estimate ~ dataset) +
  labs(x = "Estimate as a ratio to the `measured` analysis (log scale)",
       y = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = arm_cols, guide = "none") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 9) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(), legend.position = "none")

Figure 7. Estimated ErC10, ErC50 and NSEC from each convention on the four real datasets, expressed as a ratio to the measured analysis of the same dataset, with 95% credible intervals. The vertical line at 1 is exact agreement. Open symbols mark estimates flagged as unusable, meaning the interval reached an edge of the tested concentration range, where the bound is the design rather than the data, or collapsed to a point. Intervals extending past the plotted range are clipped at the panel edge.

No estimate in Figure 7 is flagged unusable: every interval lies inside the tested concentration range.

Three features of Figure 7 require care in what they do and do not establish.

First, the choice of convention changes the reported value substantially on one of the four datasets, and hardly at all on the other three. On c_proliferum the five conventions other than measured return an ErC50 between 0.72 and 0.77 times the measured estimate, which is the difference between one regulatory value and another. On c_proliferum2, r_salina and r_salina2 the estimate from the convention furthest from measured is 0.96, 1.02 and 0.87 times the measured estimate, respectively.

The size of the effect therefore does not appear to be predictable from the data alone, and on three of these four datasets a reader choosing between conventions would have seen almost no difference. However, this is not evidence that the choice is safe. The simulation is unambiguous about the direction of the error, and about the fact that the error does not shrink as an experiment becomes more precise. A single real dataset, by contrast, cannot separate the effect of a convention from the error of the analysis it is compared against, because the measured analysis has its own error and there is no truth against which to score either of them.

censored 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.00
deleted 0.50 0.41 0.43 0.60
floored 0.61 0.74 0.64 0.44
beta 0.05 0.01 0.00 0.00
gamma 0.19 0.00 0.00 0.00

Second, the mixing of some of these fits needs to be read alongside the ratios. Each fit is an average over thirteen or fourteen equations, and on two datasets a substantial share of the weight is on equations that mixed poorly. For each fit, the transcribed table records the weight held by equations whose tail effective sample size fell below 400, which is the level at which the bounds of a 95% interval are no longer reliably estimated (Table 4).

Table 4. Model weight held by equations whose tail effective sample size fell below 400, for the fits where it exceeds 0.01. Fits not listed hold essentially none. In the simulation the largest such figure in any cell and convention is under 0.005.
Dataset Convention weight on tail ESS < 400
r_salina deleted 0.576
r_salina measured 0.524
c_proliferum measured 0.151
r_salina gamma 0.065
r_salina2 deleted 0.028

This is a limitation of these four fits, and not of the conventions. It affects measured and deleted on r_salina, which are reference analyses and not the conventions under test, so the ratios on that dataset should be read as the weaker evidence. The simulation does not have this problem. Averaged over its 4,200 fits, equations failing either diagnostic account for 0.4% of the model weight, and the largest figure for any one cell and convention is 5.2% (under gamma in the ctl cell), so no figure reported from the simulation depends on an equation that did not converge.

Third, the weight on the zero-asymptote equations, which Section 5.7 identifies as a diagnostic for flooring under an unbounded family, can be computed here because it needs no truth (Table 5). Averaged over the four datasets floored places 61% of its weight on these equations, against 0% under measured and 0% under censored, whereas in the simulation the corresponding weights range from near zero to near one. Two things differ between the simulation and the case studies. In the simulation the generating equation is in the candidate set and is known to be correct, so a retaining convention recovers it and a floored one visibly cannot, whereas on real data no candidate is known to be correct. In addition, these growth-rate curves appear to decline toward zero whatever is done to the data, so a zero-asymptote shape is a defensible description of all four datasets, and not an artefact of one convention. The case studies therefore establish that the choice of convention changes the reported value, but they do not confirm the mechanism, and without a known truth they cannot.

7 Recommendations

We recommend analysing the growth rates as measured, and letting the model set determine the shape of the curve, because nothing in a Gaussian concentration-response fit requires the response to be positive. In the simulation this approach recovers the true ErC50 to within 0.6% at each level of measurement precision tested, maintains nominal interval coverage, and gives the generating equation 0.85 of the model weight at the highest precision tested.

Where the negative values were never recorded, we recommend declaring them censored instead of substituting a value. At the highest precision tested, censored matches the measurements themselves on ErC50 (-0.2% against -0.2%), and it is the only option when the underlying values are gone. Together with deleted, it is also one of only two conventions that maintain nominal coverage for all three toxicity estimates across the whole precision sweep.

Deleting the negative rows is better than replacing them, but worse than keeping them. The ErC50 bias of deleted converges on zero as the experiment becomes more precise, and its coverage remains nominal. However, deletion changes the replication per concentration, and at the top of a series it may remove a treatment group altogether, which is a change to the design and not to the data.

We do not recommend replacing negative values with zero. Flooring results in an ErC50 bias of -2.3% that does not shrink as the experiment becomes more precise, so its interval coverage falls to 0.24 at the highest precision tested, and it displaces the NSEC by -52.9%. Averaging over the candidate set absorbs part of this distortion (the ErC10 of floored is close to unbiased), but it does not remove it, and it cannot do so, because the floored data are no longer draws from the process that produced the measurements.

We also do not recommend choosing a zero-bounded response distribution (e.g. a Beta or a Gamma) as a way of dealing with negative values. Although this appears to be the most common response to negative growth rates, it does not work. The Beta maintains an ErC50 bias near -5.8% at each precision, and an ErC10 bias that increases to 9.3% as the experiment becomes more precise, while the Gamma converges on ErC50 but displaces ErC10 by -25.0%, with coverage of 0.01. Both conventions give no outward sign of a problem, as all 1,400 fits under these two conventions converged and returned all three toxicity estimates.

Converting the response to percent inhibition before fitting is also not recommended. Expressing the response as a percentage of the control caps it at 100%, which makes negative growth look like an error and may encourage the analyst to choose a bounded family. In addition, ecx(type = "absolute") already expresses the effect relative to the fitted control, so the transformation is unnecessary as well as harmful, and Ritz et al. (2026) reach this conclusion by a different route. bayesnec will warn if it detects data that appear to have been normalised.

We recommend reporting the proportion of observations at or below zero, because it is the single number that indicates whether the question arises for a dataset at all. In the ctl cell, where about two observations in seventy are negative, the four Gaussian conventions span 0.4 percentage points of ErC50 bias between them, whereas at one in seven, with equal control variability, they span 3.0.

Interval coverage and interval width should not be reported on their own. At the highest precision tested, gamma achieves nominal coverage on ErC50 with intervals 2.14 times as wide as those of measured, while floored has narrower intervals than gamma and contains the truth in a quarter of the realisations. Either figure on its own would therefore reverse the ranking of these two conventions.

Finally, the model weights should be read as a description of the data supplied. On floored data the generating equation receives essentially none of the weight, and a zero-asymptote shape receives almost all of it, with a confidence that increases as the experiment becomes more precise. A weight is evidence about which shape fits the data supplied to the model, and not about which process produced the measurements.

8 Limitations

The data are generated from a single equation (nec4param), which is in the candidate set of each Gaussian convention, so the study measures how well each convention allows a correctly specified candidate to be recovered. It does not establish what happens when no candidate is correct, which is typically the situation with real data.

The residual scale is constant along the curve, and each fit is homoscedastic to match. This is a deliberate simplification, made so that no convention is misspecified in its variance, but it means that none of the conventions reported here estimates a dispersion that varies along the curve. One of the four alga datasets does show a residual gradient (Section 5.2), so the homoscedastic case is not the only one that arises.

We also ran the precision sweep with a dispersion sub-model, on the cells and realisations used above, but do not report those results. A sub-model does not repair the conventions that impose the zero boundary through the response distribution, and adding one to a Gaussian family, whose variance model is already correct, gives its variance a gradient the data do not have. The code and the tables are in the compendium, and its CLAUDE.md records why they are not cited.

The priors are the defaults of bnec(), derived once per cell and convention from a reference realisation and then held fixed across the 100 realisations of that cell, so that the Stan programs are identical between realisations and compile only once. Holding the priors fixed eliminates the variation in the prior from one realisation to the next, which is nuisance variation. Each convention still has its own prior derived from its own prepared data, so the contrast between conventions is unaffected. Under the pinned version of bayesnec the default nec prior is a lognormal on the log of the predictor, with a central 95% interval that spans the concentrations tested. This prior places the true nec of 1.3 between the 23rd and the 63rd percentile, depending on the cell, and the true ErC50 between the 80th and the 95th, so both are comfortably inside it.

This was not the case in the version of this study published before, in which the default nec and ec50 prior was a gamma whose spread is tied to its shape. Its central 95% interval therefore covered a fraction of a logarithmically spaced series, however the series was designed, and it placed the true ErC50 above the 99th percentile in each cell. Anyone comparing both versions should therefore be aware that the equations parameterised by ec50 are likely to behave differently between them for that reason alone.

Each cell was simulated 100 times, and the Monte Carlo standard error of the reported bias has a median of 0.4% of the true value for ErC50, 1.2% for ErC10 and 2.2% for the NSEC, with a maximum of 10.5% for the gamma NSEC in the d2 cell. Differences smaller than these are not resolved by this study. The Monte Carlo standard error on a coverage of 0.95 is 0.02.

The design is fixed at seventy observations across twelve concentrations spanning a factor of one hundred, with ten controls. The study therefore does not establish how the conventions behave on a smaller design, on an arithmetic series, or, beyond the single ctl cell, on a series that does not reach the zero crossing at all.

The case studies compare the conventions on four datasets whose truth is unknown. They show that the choice of convention changes the reported value, and the results that they do not reproduce from the simulation are described in Section 6.2. However, they are not recommendations for how those particular tests should be analysed, and the Rhodomonas comparison is weaker than the Cladocopium comparison, because no convention there is a true analysis of the measurements (Section 6.1).

9 Provenance of the reported results

Neither the simulation nor the case studies are run when this vignette is built. Together they comprise 4,224 model-averaged fits, which is far more machine time than a package build can use, and they are run instead in a separate research compendium, open-AIMS/negative-response-conventions (Fisher 2026). The compendium contains the generating code, the runners, the fixed priors (as tracked files), the container in which the fits ran, and the result tables from which all figures here are transcribed.

All figures quoted are transcribed from the output of the compendium at the commit named in its bibliography entry, i.e. results/metrics.csv for the simulation, results/weights.csv for the model weights of Table 2, and results/case_estimates.csv for Section 6. The fits were run against bayesnec at commit 9269bf6d, as recorded in the compendium’s hpc/bayesnec.lock, inside the container identified by the compendium’s hpc/image.lock, which provides the toolchain and installs the package from that pinned source.

This commit is a development version of bayesnec, and not a release. The version is more important here than usual, because this vignette measures the behaviour of the package defaults. The results reported above depend on three defaults at that commit: the nec and ec50 priors are built on the log of the predictor, the initial-value search accepts chains individually, and the NSEC crossing is sought from the control upward, with the control as the first point of the searched grid. The NSEC search was revised after that commit in ways that may change NSEC estimates and their intervals (see NEWS.md), so an analysis run under a later version of bayesnec may not reproduce these numbers exactly.

The posterior predictive figures quoted in Section 5.4 are transcribed from results/ppc_spread.csv, which summarises 100 realisations of each cell and convention, and cover only the four precision cells. The study also keeps one fitted object per cell and convention, and all 24 case fits, chosen by a seed fixed on the cell and convention names before any result was seen. These fits are not in the compendium’s repository (66 model-averaged fits is too much to track), and are instead fetched from the cluster with hpc/fetch-fits.sh.

The case studies are also fitted in the compendium. Four datasets by six conventions, each an average over thirteen or fourteen equations, take about fifteen hours, which is too long to run on a workstation whenever the vignette is built. The case-study estimates therefore describe the pinned commit, as the simulation does, and not the version of bayesnec installed with this vignette. However, Table 3, which describes the four datasets themselves, is computed at build time from the alga data that ship with the package, and therefore does reflect your installation.
